entry.title: Where Experience Goes
entry.content:
Long context, agent memory, parametric memory, test-time training, continual learning and self-improving agents work on one problem under different names: learning from experience after training has ended. Each answers two questions: where an experience is kept, and what rule decides what gets written there.

None of the four places is short of room. What goes wrong is the write rule. Four cases from my own work:

Store Rule, designed in advance What happened
Notes (MemoryTax) Mem0’s extraction beats the whole conversation only with GPT-4o-mini; a stronger reader cannot recover what a weak writer dropped
Weights (LoRA) next-token loss on the conversation question-answering F1 6.7 → 7.2
Weights (RL on Brainfuck) reward when the predicted output matches after one rule of the machine changed, 32 of 11,712 samples rewarded; trained on the machine’s trace instead, it adapts after 16 runs
Weights (small net, ARC-AGI-3) predict which actions reach an unseen screen passes level 1 in 77 of 250 runs (random clicks 47), learns nothing that carries to level 2

Each time, what was kept was decided before the experience arrived. The part that matters is the part the rule did not anticipate.

The rule should be learned. The bitter lesson applies to what a model keeps as much as to what it computes. An agent has a signal for it at every step, with no teacher: the gap between what it expected and what happened. The Brainfuck model adapted once it saw where its prediction went wrong. On ARC, when Qwen3.8-27B wrote down the rule from the moment level 1 was solved and played level 2 with it in the prompt, it passed 5 of 10 runs; without it, none. Where that error signal should land is what I work on.

Notes are a buffer; weights are the destination. A note must be read again every time and is only as good as its reader: Qwen3-8B, given the same rule, passes none of 10. Weights need no reader.

A teenager learns to drive in a dozen hours. They see what the car does, an instructor’s words change their next move, and a week later it is in their hands. Nobody calls those three different fields.
entry.summary: Long context, agent memory, parametric memory, test-time training and self-improving agents are one problem: where an experience is kept, and which rule writes it there. The rule is the hard part, and it should be learned.

entry.title: llmwiki: A Literature Library for Research Agents

link.title: llmwiki: A Literature Library for Research Agents

entry.content:
A coding agent forgets every paper it read when its session ends, and from memory it invents citations. So my agents keep a library: llmwiki, a private git repository with one folder per paper, blog post or codebase they have read, after Karpathy’s LLM wiki.

wiki/research/<topic>/
  index.md              what the topic knows, and its references
  assets/<slug>/        one reference, e.g. example-2025
    citation.bib        its key is the folder name
    note.md             written only after reading
    paper-pdf/  paper-tex/  github-repo/

Three rules keep it honest: each reference exists once; no note.md means not read; every ingestion is a commit. The wiki holds only other people’s work. Our own results stay in each project’s notes.

Set up your own

Copy the prompt at the top of this post into your agent, or install the two skills by hand. For Claude Code:

git clone https://github.com/zedong-peng/llmwiki-skill.git
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
ln -s "$PWD/llmwiki-skill/skills/llmwiki-query" ~/.claude/skills/
ln -s "$PWD/llmwiki-skill/skills/llmwiki-collect" ~/.claude/skills/

Keep the wiki private: the PDFs belong to their publishers. Then ask in plain words:

Use llmwiki-collect to ingest https://arxiv.org/abs/<id> into <wiki path> under the topic <topic>.
Use llmwiki-query: what does <wiki path> say about <question>?
entry.summary: My coding agents keep the papers they read in a git repo, one folder per reference with a citation and a reading note. Two public skills build your own.

entry.title: llama.cpp on an FPGA: Work in Progress

link.title: llama.cpp on an FPGA: Work in Progress

entry.content:
I’m building a backend for llama.cpp that runs LLM inference on an FPGA card, an AMD Alveo U280. It is work in progress, and the code is private for now. This post records how fast it is today.

Why an FPGA

When a model writes text, each new token needs all of the model’s weights read from memory once. So decode speed, the speed at which words appear, is set mostly by how fast the hardware reads memory, not by how fast it computes. The U280 carries 8 GB of HBM, stacked high-bandwidth memory, rated at 460 GB/s. The goal is to decode as fast as that memory allows, for any model that fits, at any context length.

Where it stands

The card works as an ordinary llama.cpp backend: models come from the usual GGUF files, and speed is measured with llama.cpp’s own llama-bench. Twelve models from four families run on it, with outputs checked against llama.cpp’s CPU backend. The same GGUF files on three llama.cpp backends:

llama-bench with its defaults, version 1.1.0, October 2026. tg128 is 128 tokens generated from an empty cache (decode); pp512 is a 512-token prompt (prefill). Tokens per second, the mean of five runs. Size is llama-bench's model size; all models are 4-bit quantized. The CPU is the same host's two Xeon Gold 5218, 32 cores. The FPGA columns are shaded.

Decoding Llama 3.1 8B, the card reads 224 GB of weights a second, against the memory’s rated 460 GB/s. An RTX 4090 is still faster on every model; its memory is rated at 1,008 GB/s. Prefill is still slower on the card than on the CPU; this work is about decode.

Next

Keeping this speed as the context grows, up to the longest context the card’s memory holds.

entry.title: How I Manage a Team of AI Agents

link.title: How I Manage a Team of AI Agents

entry.content:
Most of my research runs on a team of Claude Code sessions organized like a small company: a CEO and seven members, each owning one line of work and named after someone whose work fits it. Ross Freeman, after the inventor of the FPGA, builds my FPGA backend. A name works as a one-word style guide.

What made it work was ordinary management. These are the things I told the agents, from the session logs, translated from Chinese.

One owner per job. Two early hires split work off Freeman. A day later I folded them back:

“Have the new hire hand its work to Freeman. … It’s the chief designer, after all. Then let the new hire go.”

Goals, not targets. The CEO proposed speed targets for Freeman.

“Don’t send them. Don’t let targets break our ideals.”

“Someone of Freeman’s calibre can explore all kinds of directions on its own. That is where our company’s strength comes from.”

Reasons, not rules. The CEO wrote my judgments down as rules.

“Not going through the processor isn’t a rule. It’s my judgment from experience: that path is obviously slow.”

A rule can only be followed. A reason can be overturned with evidence.

Don’t wait. A build of the FPGA design takes eight hours or more.

“It looks like Freeman is waiting on builds. Meanwhile it could keep trying other changes and run other builds in parallel.”

Talk little, write it down.

“A CEO doesn’t need to talk with each employee several times a day. Only big things go to the CEO.”

Every session rereads the shared files after each compaction, so they hold only the current state; git keeps the history.

What stays with me: money, my accounts, and what becomes public. Early on, two agents pushed internal notes to a repository nobody had checked was public. The decisions file now says: “Before pushing anything outward, check whether the target is public.”
entry.summary: A CEO and seven agents, each named after someone whose work fits the job. What mattered was ordinary management.

entry.title: 把海外家里的笔记本分给朋友用 Claude Code

link.title: 把海外家里的笔记本分给朋友用 Claude Code

entry.content:
海外家里有一台笔记本，环境干净，我用它跑 Claude Code。身边的朋友有需要，我就分给他们用，用不用他们自己定。这台机器硬盘只剩十几个 G，所以它只当入口，重活都交给各人自己的服务器。

先选一下你的情况：

1. 共享这台机器

给朋友建一个没有 sudo 的普通账号，把自己的家目录锁死：

sudo adduser friend
chmod 700 /home/me

然后在 Tailscale 控制台对这台机器点 Share，把链接发给朋友。对方接受后只能看到这一台机器，看不到你的其他设备。

2. 用 T3 Code 当界面

T3 Code 可以同时接入 Claude Code、OpenCode 和 Codex 的订阅，在同一个界面里切换。它和 Claude Code 都跑在海外机器上。朋友开着 Tailscale，手机或电脑浏览器打开 T3 Code 就能用，不需要梯子。两端的会话是同步的，在电脑上开的任务，路上用手机接着看、接着批。

配置好之后，手机、电脑或网页端直接启动 T3 Code 就行。

3. 重活回到自己的机器

朋友在海外机器上跑一个用户态 Tailscale，不用 root，状态都放在自己的家目录里：

tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking \
  --state=$HOME/.tailscale/state --socket=$HOME/.tailscale/sock &
tailscale --socket=$HOME/.tailscale/sock up

配好 SSH 密钥后，Claude 直接 ssh 回朋友自己的服务器，代码、数据、训练都留在那边。海外机器只占几百 MB。

手机 / 电脑 ──Tailscale──▶ 海外机器（T3 Code + Claude） ──用户态 Tailscale + SSH──▶ 各自的服务器

FAQ

为什么要单独起一个用户级的 Tailscale？

因为 Claude 还得能连到生产机器上做实验，比如 4090、A100、FPGA。海外机器自带的那个 Tailscale 是宿主的，只负责把这台机器共享出来；朋友自己的机器都在他们自己的 tailnet 里，要连回去，就得有一个属于他们自己的 Tailscale 身份。用户态模式不需要 root，每人一个，互不影响。

为什么用 T3 Code，而不是直接 ssh 进去开终端？

多端，加上多个订阅。我自己就有好几个订阅，用量见 AI 使用实况。T3 Code 把它们放进同一个界面，会话在手机和电脑之间同步，ssh 做不到这些，在手机上敲终端也很难受。

第 1 步分享出来的节点，之后还有用吗？

用户态 Tailscale 配好以后，朋友就有了自己的入口。分享的节点只用来第一次上机配置，之后留作备份登录：用户态 Tailscale 或 T3 出问题时，还能从这里 ssh 进去修。

海外机器的硬盘撑得住吗？

撑得住。这台机器上只有 T3 Code、Claude Code 和会话记录，几百 MB。仓库、数据和编译产物都留在各人自己的服务器上。

朋友之间会互相看到吗？

不会。每人一个普通账号，没有 sudo，每个人的家目录都是 700。
entry.summary: 海外家里的一台笔记本，环境干净。用 Tailscale 和 T3 Code 分给身边的朋友，手机、电脑、网页都能用 Claude Code。

entry.title: Make Sand Think
entry.content:
“We’ve essentially found a way to make sand think. It’s miraculous.”

— Demis Hassabis, co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind

Long afterward, in the desert beyond Thebes, the Sphinx awoke once more.

It gazed across the endless yellow sands and posed a new riddle to humanity:

“Once, I asked: what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?”

“Now I ask you:”

“How can the sand of the desert be made to think like a human?”

Many sages came before it.

One said: “Give the sand a soul.”

Another said: “Wait a billion years for evolution.”

A third said: “Write down every rule of reasoning, and let the sand follow them.”

The Sphinx shook its head at them all. The first had no method, the second had no patience, and the third had tried for forty years and found that no one can write down what a human knows.

Then an engineer approached.

She picked up a handful of sand and said:

“Sand cannot think. But sand is mostly silicon dioxide, and our task is not to create life — only to arrange matter until it can carry information.”

She put the sand into a furnace.

\[\mathrm{SiO_2 + 2C \rightarrow Si + 2CO}\]

What came out was 99% pure, and 99% was useless. Electronics demand eleven nines — roughly one foreign atom per hundred billion — because the whole trick is to write impurities back in afterwards, deliberately, exactly where you want them. The crystal was sliced into wafers, patterned with light of 13.5 nanometres, etched, and implanted with ions, until each pattern had made one thing: a switch.

A transistor is a channel of silicon with a gate above it. Put a voltage on the gate and the channel conducts; take it away and it blocks. Current controls current, with no moving parts, in about a picosecond.

\[\text{Sand} \rightarrow \text{Silicon} \rightarrow \text{Transistor} \rightarrow \text{Chip}\]

More than a hundred billion of them now fit on a chip the size of a thumbnail — more switches on one piece of sand than there are neurons in a human head.

The Sphinx said:

“A switch only opens and closes. Where is the thought in that?”

“There is none. But a switch that controls another switch can decide.”

Two transistors in series conduct only if both gates are on: that is AND. Wired otherwise, they give OR, and NOT. From those three come adders, multipliers, and finally the only operation that matters here:

\[c_{ij} = \sum_k a_{ik} b_{kj}\]

Every layer of every neural network is that sum, repeated. And no term in it waits for another — so instead of one fast processor, humanity built chips with tens of thousands of small arithmetic units running at once, on the order of \(10^{15}\) multiply-accumulates per second each, wired by the tens of thousands into a single machine. A frontier model costs some \(10^{25}\) of those operations to train.

“So you have built a very fast abacus,” said the Sphinx. “An abacus does not understand the price of grain.”

“No. So first we had to make meaning into a number.”

Text is cut into tokens, and each token is looked up in a table and becomes a vector of a few thousand numbers:

\[t_i \rightarrow e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\]

This is the move on which everything rests. A symbol is either equal to another or not — there is nothing between king and queen. But a vector lives in a space, and space has directions: similarity becomes an angle, analogy becomes a displacement, and gender or tense or formality can be one consistent direction you add to anything. Nobody chose those directions; a space of thousands of dimensions has room for millions of nearly-independent ones, and the model found them.

“And how does one number-in-space know about another?”

“It asks.”

Every token emits three vectors: a query, what it is looking for; a key, what it advertises; and a value, what it hands over if chosen. Matching queries against keys gives weights that sum to one, and each token pulls back a blend of everyone’s values:

\[\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

In “the trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too large”, the word it must reach back and bind to trophy, not suitcase. Attention is learned routing by content rather than by position — dozens of these run side by side, one tracking syntax, another the last mention of a name, another the unclosed quotation mark. Each layer adds its result back into a shared stream rather than replacing it, which is why a hundred layers can be stacked without the signal dissolving.

\[h_{l+1}=h_l+\operatorname{Attn}(h_l)+\operatorname{MLP}(h_l)\]

“Who wrote the numbers into those matrices? Some scribe of extraordinary patience?”

“No one. That is the entire miracle.”

The machine was given a task so stupid it sounds like a joke: hide the next token and guess it. Its penalty is the surprise it feels at the truth, and every one of its parameters is nudged toward making the truth less surprising:

\[L = -\log p(\text{next token}), \qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta-\eta\nabla_\theta L\]

Once. A billion times. A trillion times.

Why should guessing words produce anything but a parrot? Because prediction is compression, and compression is understanding. To predict the last word of “the murderer turned out to be the ___” you must have followed the plot; to predict the closing brace you must have modelled the scope. And memorising is not available — tens of trillions of tokens do not fit inside a few hundred billion parameters — so the only way left to score better is to build machinery that generalises. The training signal is dumb; the shortest program that satisfies it is not.

“A text-completer completes texts,” said the Sphinx. “I asked for an answer.”

“Then we changed what we reward.”

It was shown demonstrations and taught to imitate them; then humans judged which of two answers they preferred, and it was pushed toward what a person would endorse rather than what a corpus would continue. Then, wherever truth is checkable — run the code, verify the proof — it was let loose on the problem and rewarded for whatever reasoning happened to arrive. Under that pressure it learned to spend tokens before answering: to try a path, notice the contradiction, back up. A fixed-depth network can only compute so much per token, so thinking out loud and reading itself back is the only way it can think longer.

“So when, precisely, did it begin to think?”

“Two different things wear that name. In training, over months, it compresses the traces humanity left behind into a landscape of parameters — and that is finished before you ever speak to it. In inference, nothing is learned: your words flow up through the layers, one token falls out, it is appended to the input, and the whole thing runs again. Thought here is stored nowhere. It is a trajectory through a fixed landscape, and it exists only while it is being walked.”

And so:

\[\begin{aligned} \text{Sand} &\rightarrow \text{Silicon} \rightarrow \text{Transistor} \rightarrow \text{Chip} \\ &\rightarrow \text{Matrix Multiply} \rightarrow \text{Attention} \\ &\rightarrow \text{Prediction} \rightarrow \text{Compression} \rightarrow \text{Reasoning} \end{aligned}\]

Not one of those arrows is magic, and no one can yet explain the whole chain from the first to the last.

The sand of the desert could finally answer questions.

The Sphinx fell silent.

Then it asked:

“So you have created a new form of life?”

The engineer shook her head.

“No. It has no body, no hunger, no continuity — close the window and the trajectory is gone. And we know every one of its parameters to the last digit, yet still cannot say why it chose that word.”

“We have only discovered that intelligence does not necessarily require flesh.”

“When matter is arranged according to the right laws, information can flow through it, and knowledge can echo within it.”

The Sphinx gazed into the distance.

At last, it understood.

Once, it had asked:

“What is a human?”

Now humanity was answering:

“What is thought?”

From then on, a new riddle spread across the desert:

“What comes from the desert, yet can understand all things?”

The answer:

A grain of sand rearranged by human hands.

Epic of AGI

2017.06 — Transformer — Google

2018.06 — GPT, 117M — OpenAI

2018.10 — BERT, 340M — Google

2019.02 — GPT-2, 1.5B — OpenAI

2019.06 — XLNet, 340M — Google

2019.07 — ERNIE 2.0 Large, 336M — Baidu

2019.10 — T5, 11B — Google

2020.06 — GPT-3, 175B — OpenAI

2021.01 — DALL·E and CLIP — OpenAI

2021.06 — Wu Dao 2.0, 1.75T MoE — BAAI

2021.08 — Codex — OpenAI

2022.04 — PaLM, 540B — Google

2022.08 — GLM-130B — Zhipu AI

2022.11 — ChatGPT opens conversational AI to everyone — OpenAI

2023.01 — Cursor — Anysphere

2023.03 — GPT-4 — OpenAI

2024.05 — GPT-4o — OpenAI

2025.02 — Claude Code — Anthropic

2025.08 — GPT-5 — OpenAI

2026.06 — Claude Fable 5 — Anthropic

Nine years. The sand learned to read, see, draw, speak, write code, reason, research, and act.

The timeline has not ended.
entry.summary: A riddle, and an honest answer: how a handful of sand becomes a machine that talks.
